title: Shipping a massive MMO patch solo with AI: how I built player-run AFK shops, on-the-fly MMO slang translation, and shader skin tones in a custom TypeScript/Babylon.js engine (Velundra v1.0.6)
author: GastonSaillen
selftext:
One of the hardest parts of building a browser-based 3D MMORPG from scratch in pure TypeScript and Babylon.js isn't the initial prototype—it's maintaining velocity once live players are hitting the server every day.

I just pushed **v1.0.6** for **Velundra** (`velundra.io/devlog.html#v1-0-6`), which ended up being one of the largest content and systems updates since opening the alpha. Using Claude Code heavily inside my local workflow has completely changed how I scope patches, moving me away from "spend two weeks wiring boilerplate" toward rapid iteration on server-authoritative edge cases.

Instead of dumping raw patch notes, here is what actually went into building the core systems of 1.0.6 with AI in the loop—and where AI still falls flat on its face in multiplayer game dev:

**1. Server-Authoritative AFK Player Shops** Classic MMOs live or die by their player economy, so I added personal stalls at level 20 (`/shop` or via the inventory tab). Players can list up to 8 items, set prices, and go AFK with a golden scale sign overhead while level 15+ players buy in one click.

* **The AI workflow:** AI is phenomenal at cranking out UI state machines—like the 4-step interactive onboarding tutorial, auto-docking the trade window so it never overlaps the bag, and wiring up the `- / +` stack selectors.
* **Where I had to step in:** Race conditions and economy exploits. Left alone, LLM-generated transaction handlers are notorious for subtle duplication vectors when two buyers click the same stack on the same server tick, or when a seller tries to equip an item currently listed in their stall. I had to manually enforce the server-side locks, the 50% vendor-value price floor, and the confirmation guards.

**2. Real-Time Chat Translation That Understands MMO Shorthand** Because the server sits in South America but pulls players from both English- and Spanish-speaking communities, language barriers were killing party formation. I added an experimental auto-translate toggle in `Options → Accessibility` along with stacked overhead chat bubbles so adjacent players don't clip their text.

* **The interesting wrinkle:** Standard translation pipelines butcher gaming slang. Getting the prompt and glossary layer right so it translates `wtb`, `wts`, `lfg`, `omw`, and `brb` naturally in context—while attaching a small `Tt` badge to inspect the original message—took way more tuning than the WebSocket plumbing itself.

**3. Shader Skin Tones, Pet Satiety, and Combat Feel** A big focus of 1.0.6 was making the world feel less rigid and removing friction from questing:

* **Skin tones & interactive benches:** Added five skin tones at character creation. Doing this cleanly in Babylon.js meant isolating the skin shader channels so armor, shirts, and trousers stay untinted when unequipped. I also added interactive benches across Lumbrera and the Oath Bastion where your character walks up, turns, and sits down.
* **Pet satiety & action bar treats:** Pets now have a 0–100% satiety meter that only drains while hunting outside safe zones (never offline or in town). As they get hungry, their 3D aura dims, and you can slot treats onto keys `8`, `9`, or `0` to feed them mid-fight without breaking stride.
* **Visual & quest reworks:** Completely rebuilt *Round of Souls* (6 comet-tailed souls, inner spirits, spinning double ground runes), added rarity-framed item cards with large painted icons across all 407 items (now shareable via `velundra.io/items.html`), and fixed the classic MMO bottleneck where quest elites like *Pale Claw* had 30-minute respawn timers—now they spawn within 5 seconds if you arrive on their active quest step.

**A question for others building multiplayer games with AI:** How are you handling authoritative server validation and state synchronization in your AI workflows? I've found AI saves me \~70% of the time on client-side 3D visuals, UI plumbing, and tooling, but the moment distributed state or anti-cheat/economy invariants are involved, reviewing AI code takes almost as long as writing it from scratch. Have you found good patterns or test harnesses to keep AI-written netcode trustworthy?

Another question... 

Did anyone worked with character customization sets? how is your AI workflow on that part?
